sources: **State mid-term report** for the third cycle (2022-2024)
meta.headline: **Partial implementation (B)** is the dominant outcome (110 of 222 recommendations) alongside a large block of **No relevant action (C)** (93 recommendations). B reflects concrete measures in the National Report: the Commission on Human Rights and Public Administration Bill introduced in Parliament (2026), the Legal Aid Act (2025), a reconstituted Judicial Service Commission, the National Disability Plan of Action 2024-2028 and a National Disability Advisory Council, a GBV Coordination Mechanism, the Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health and Nutrition Strategy 2024-2028, education reforms (primary dropout down from 6.5% to 4.8%) and higher social grants. C persists on ratification (OP-CAT, OP-CEDAW, the Second Optional Protocol and others), the death penalty, same-sex relations and anti-discrimination law for sexual orientation and gender identity, corporal punishment, the Family Law Bills (the Marriages Bill is still not enacted, so the marriage age stays at 16), political parties, torture and accountability for the 2021 unrest and the killing of Thulani Maseko. **Contrary measures (E)** apply to seven recommendations: the Government obtained a Supreme Court judgment (August 2024) upholding the Suppression of Terrorism Act and the Sedition and Subversive Activities Act and made no reform, and the UN reports excessive force against protests. The National Report refers water and sanitation, gender-based violence and inclusive education to the State mid-term report (2022-2024), which was also used: it records rural water schemes, solar-powered pumps and disability-accessible water facilities (**B** on water and sanitation).

blocks.summary: Ensure the right to peaceful assembly and investigate violations
blocks.rationale: The State's review of the June 2021 unrest found no unlawful conduct by police; the UN country team reports excessive force against peaceful assemblies and stalled investigations.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 39 — Eswatini: "The outcome of these reviews did not reveal evidence of unlawful conduct on the part of police officers in the discharge of their duties"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 39 — United Nations country team: "participants in peaceful assemblies had been met with excessive force, arbitrary arrests, prolonged detention and serious injuries"

recommendations.text: Ensure the freedom of assembly, association and expression, including media freedom, online and offline

blocks.summary: End law enforcement violence against peaceful assemblies
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: The ILO reports that more than 80 people were reported to have lost their lives in police crackdowns on protests in 2022-2023 and the UN country team reports excessive force against peaceful assemblies; the State maintains the force used was necessary and proportionate.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 52 — ILO Committee of Experts: "more than 80 people were reported to have lost their lives because of police crackdowns on protests"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 39 — Eswatini: "The outcome of these reviews did not reveal evidence of unlawful conduct on the part of police officers in the discharge of their duties"

recommendations.text: Immediately end law enforcement violence and other restrictions against people exercising their rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and to freedom of association

blocks.summary: Investigate violations by security forces against protesters in 2021 and ensure accountability
blocks.rationale: The State's internal reviews found no unlawful conduct; the UN country team reports that investigations have stalled and ICJ and Amnesty call for an independent mechanism.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 38 — Eswatini: "the REPS undertook internal investigations and reviews of incidents involving the use of force during the unrest"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 24 — United Nations country team: "investigations had stalled in relation to the perpetrators of the 2021–2023 violence in which protestors, including a prominent human rights lawyer, had been killed"

recommendations.text: Investigate allegations of human rights violations by security forces against protesters between May and July 2021 and ensure accountability

themes.theme: Freedom of opinion and expression & access to information

blocks.summary: Protect freedom of expression, association and assembly
blocks.rationale: The National Report cites the Constitution and the Sibaya dialogue (2023) and states that no one is targeted; the UN country team and ICJ report that the Sedition, Terrorism and Public Order Acts are used to restrict dissent and internet services are shut down during protests.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 46 — Eswatini: "Eswatini provides a safe environment for exercising civic space rights, with no individuals targeted"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 34 — United Nations country team: "restricted debate and dissent through broad discretionary powers and criminal sanctions"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 70 — El Hak: "Eswatini recurrently resorted to completely shutting down internet services to block information during protests"

recommendations.text: Respect, protect and fulfil the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly, including by ensuring that representatives of political parties, the media and the civil society are not prohibited from exercising these rights
Develop legislation to protect the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly, including by allowing political parties to register and contest elections
Urgently adopt all necessary measures to remove the restrictions which prevent the enjoyment of the rights to freedom of expression and association, as well as media freedom
Promote and protect the right to freedom of expression and media freedom

Amend the Public Order Act of 2017 so that it fully protects the rights to freedom of expression and to peaceful association and assembly, and allow all people to express their views without fear of reprisals
Take concrete measures to guarantee civil and political rights, including civil society space and press freedom

recommendations.by: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
recommendations.text: Amend legislation which restricts freedoms of expression, association and peaceful assembly, and take steps to guarantee space for civil society actors and journalists to operate without fear of reprisals
Continue to reinforce relevant measures to promote and protect the right to freedom of expression and the right to peaceful assembly
Strengthen efforts to ensure the implementation of the right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly

blocks.summary: Repeal the 1938 Sedition and Subversive Activities Act
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: The Supreme Court upheld the Act and the Suppression of Terrorism Act in August 2024 and Eswatini cites the judgment as affirming that rights are subject to lawful limitations; the Act continues to be applied against dissent.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 47 — Eswatini: "the Supreme Court upheld the Sedition and Subversive Activities Act 46 of 1938 and Suppression of Terrorism Act 3 of 2028 as consistent with constitutional guarantees"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 34 — United Nations country team: "restricted debate and dissent through broad discretionary powers and criminal sanctions"

recommendations.text: Repeal the 1938 Sedition and Subversive Activities Act, which has been used to silence journalists, human right defenders, and political activists

blocks.summary: Reform or repeal the Suppression of Terrorism Act and the Sedition and Subversive Activities Act
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: The Prime Minister, as appellant, obtained an August 2024 Supreme Court judgment upholding both Acts and the National Report cites it as affirming that rights are subject to lawful limitations; no reform was undertaken and the Acts continue to be applied against dissent: a position contrary to the recommendation.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 47 — Eswatini: "the Supreme Court upheld the Sedition and Subversive Activities Act 46 of 1938 and Suppression of Terrorism Act 3 of 2028 as consistent with constitutional guarantees"

Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 38 — Amnesty International: "Eswatini had neither taken adequate steps to bring the Suppression of Terrorism Act into line with international standards"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 18 — United Nations country team: "the Suppression of Terrorism Act, 2008, was applied in ways that conflated terrorism with political dissent"

recommendations.text: Modify or repeal the laws which unduly restrict civil and political rights, including the Public Order Act and certain elements of the Suppression of Terrorism Act, in order to bring laws into conformity with international law relating to human rights

Reform, in accordance with international human rights standards, all legislation that unduly restricts freedom of expression and association, in particular, the Suppression of Terrorism Act and the Suppression of Sedition and Subversive Activities Act

Repeal the Suppression of Terrorism Act, 2008 as amended in 2017, to bring it in line with Eswatini’s Constitution as well as the country’s obligations under international and regional human rights law

Reform expeditiously the Suppression of Terrorism Act and the Sedition and Subversive Activities Act so that they cannot be used to undermine the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly

blocks.summary: Reform the judiciary and strengthen its independence
blocks.rationale: The Judicial Service Commission was reconstituted by Legal Notice (2025) and additional judges and magistrates were appointed; ICJ and El Hak report executive interference and low public confidence.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 18 — Eswatini: "members of the Judicial Service Commission were appointed through Legal Notice of 2025"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 40 — ICJ: "public confidence in the judiciary in Eswatini was very low"

recommendations.text: Intensify the reform of the judicial system
Implement constitutional protections to ensure the independence of the judiciary and Parliament
Fully implement Constitutional provisions in order to ensure the enjoyment of the right to freedom of expression and the independence of the judiciary and the Parliament

blocks.summary: Fight impunity of security forces
blocks.rationale: The State's internal reviews of the June 2021 unrest found no unlawful police conduct; the UN country team and Amnesty report stalled investigations and impunity.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 39 — Eswatini: "The outcome of these reviews did not reveal evidence of unlawful conduct on the part of police officers in the discharge of their duties"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 43 — Amnesty International: "failures to investigate unlawful killings such as the killing of human rights lawyer Thulani Maseko"

recommendations.text: Strengthen the fight against impunity of members of the security forces in the event of manifest violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms

themes.theme: Right to participate in public affairs & right to vote

blocks.summary: Allow political parties and reform the electoral system
blocks.rationale: The National Report describes only the Elections and Boundaries Commission and civic education; political parties remain banned and the People's United Democratic Movement was designated a terrorist organisation.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 52 — Eswatini: "The Elections and Boundaries Commission (EBC) is established by Section 90 of the Constitution and the Elections and Boundaries Commission Act No. 3 of 2013"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 72 — JS6: "the continued legal and practical ban on political parties exemplified Eswatini’s entrenched resistance to pluralism"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 73 — JS6: "the political formation the People’s United Democratic Movement had been designated as a terrorist organization by the authorities"

recommendations.text: Lift the ban on the registration of political parties
Revise the electoral system in order to allow political parties to participate in elections
Guarantee free and fair elections by ensuring the independence of bodies responsible for elections and anti-corruption
Consider reviewing the King’s Decree on political parties
Revoke the decree banning political parties, and allow the registration and operation of political parties

Formally declare to the people of Eswatini that the 2005 Constitution revoked the ban on political parties under the 1973 Decree, and work with civil society to draft regulations to the Elections Act that clarify how political parties and party-affiliated candidates are permitted to participate in the electoral space

Revise the Constitution and other laws and policies by its next universal periodic review in order to allow forming of political parties and facilitating all forms of participation in political and public life in line with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights

blocks.summary: Youth participation in political decision-making
blocks.rationale: The Elections and Boundaries Commission runs civic and voter education for young people through social media and national events.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 53 — Eswatini: "thereby expanding access to information, particularly among young people"

recommendations.text: Strengthen the participation of young people in political decision-making processes

blocks.summary: Strengthen health services and HIV response
blocks.rationale: Eswatini provides free long-acting PrEP, runs the HIV Stigma Index and adopted an NCD and mental health plan 2024-2028; life expectancy rose from 58.2 to 64.5 years; the Committee on the Rights of the Child notes scarce rural facilities and medicine stock-outs.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 90 — Eswatini: "life expectancy rates have increased to 64.5 years (2026) for both sexes combined from 58.2 years in 2021"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 91 — Eswatini: "National Non Communicable Diseases, Injuries and Mental Health (NCDIMH) Sector operational plan 2024-2028"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 62 — Committee on the Rights of the Child: "remained concerned about the scarcity of healthcare facilities, particularly in rural areas"

recommendations.text: Make efforts to promote the enjoyment of the right to health, guaranteeing access to quality health services, including for the treatment of HIV/AIDS, and investing in awareness-raising campaigns to ensure that all people are duly informed about the risks of transmission of this disease, as well as to combat the stigmatization associated with it
Take measures that will strengthen the health sector and provide the necessary health care and ways to reach all areas and vulnerable groups in the country
Implement measures to ensure free, universal access to health for all
Continue to enhance access to health care and programmes to address non-communicable diseases
Further intensify efforts to reduce HIV/AIDS infections
Continue its efforts to reduce the spread of HIV/AIDS
Raise public awareness about the dangers of HIV infection, including the harm associated with the stigmatization of HIV patients
Continue to respond to the challenges posed by HIV/AIDS in the country

themes.theme: Right to an adequate standard of living

blocks.summary: Promote social policies for the most vulnerable
blocks.rationale: Elderly and disability grants were increased, food assistance reached 263,090 people and a decent shelter programme built 204 houses.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 73 — Eswatini: "Elderly Grant increased by 20 per cent from E500 (USD31.25) to E600 (USD37.50) per month"

recommendations.text: Continue promoting its successful social policies to increase the quality of life of its people, in particular of the most vulnerable sectors

themes.theme: Economic, social & cultural rights - general measures of implementation

blocks.summary: Implement economic and social development programmes
blocks.rationale: The Government Programme of Action, National Development Plan 2023-2028 and regional agricultural funds target disparities.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 75 — Eswatini: "The NDP prioritises poverty reduction, food security, and inclusive economic growth"

recommendations.text: Continue the implementation of economic and social development programmes in order to reduce disparities

blocks.summary: Agricultural productivity and women's access to land
blocks.rationale: The Regional Development Fund and Agricultural Development Fund financed 107 projects (60% women beneficiaries); JS3 notes dual tenure still restricts women's land rights.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 76 — Eswatini: "the Regional Development Fund (RDF) supported 107 agricultural projects to enhance productivity and food security"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 93 — JS3: "dual tenure (Title Deed Land and Swazi Nation Land) and customary allocation practices continued to restrict women’s tenure rights"

recommendations.text: Prioritize measures to promote agricultural productivity and food security, including by ensuring women’s equitable access to land

blocks.summary: Strengthen social protection floors
blocks.rationale: The Social Security Inquiry tool (2024/25), the Eswatini National Pension Fund Bill (2025) and increased grants extend protection; only 29% of the population is covered.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 69 — Eswatini: "the Eswatini National Pension Fund (ENPF) Bill, introducing a comprehensive National Pension Scheme"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 57 — United Nations country team: "social protection coverage remained limited, with only 29% of the population covered"

recommendations.text: Strengthen social protection floors catering for the vulnerable and marginalized groups in society

blocks.summary: Improve access to safe drinking water and sanitation
blocks.rationale: The National Report refers water and sanitation to Eswatini's mid-term report, which records rural water schemes, a solar-powered pump pilot, disability-accessible water facilities and a sanitation project; the proportion with safely managed drinking water rose from 75% to 81.2% (2022-2023). The Committee on the Rights of the Child notes children in informal settlements without water.
evidence: State mid-term report (mid-term report), para. 36 — Eswatini: "The proportion of the national population which has access to safely managed clean drinking water increased from 75% in 2022 to 81.2% in 2023"
State mid-term report (mid-term report), para. 37 — Eswatini: "introducing solar- powered pumps as a renewable energy solution"
State mid-term report (mid-term report), para. 38 — Eswatini: "New facility designs now accommodate persons with disabilities (PWDs)"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 61 — Committee on the Rights of the Child: "many children lived in informal settlements without access to water or sanitation"

recommendations.text: Continue to take the necessary measures to improve access to safe and clean drinking water and sanitation facilities to the vulnerable population
Increase, significantly, investments in rural areas to fight inequalities and improve access to drinking water while addressing sanitation deficiencies in the country
Continue the initiatives Eswatini has implemented with the support of development partners to improve potable water supply and sanitation, especially in rural areas

blocks.summary: Decriminalise abortion and provide comprehensive sexuality education
blocks.rationale: The National Report states that abortion is not criminalised in cases of rape, incest, fetal malformation or risk to health or life, without citing a legal change; the CRC recommends comprehensive sexuality education in the compulsory curriculum.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 104 — Eswatini: "Eswatini does not criminalise abortion in cases of rape, incest, serious fetal malformation, or risks to the health or life of the pregnant woman"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 69 — Committee on the Rights of the Child: "ensure that comprehensive sexual and reproductive health education was part of the compulsory school curriculum"

recommendations.text: Decriminalize abortion and guarantee the provision of, and access to, comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services and goods, including safe abortion and post-abortion care, and modern contraceptives

Decriminalize abortion and guarantee the provision of, and access to, comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services and goods, including safe abortion and post-abortion care, and modern contraceptives
Repeal laws that do not allow safe abortions, affordable contraceptives, or reproductive rights
Provide access to comprehensive sexuality education as part of the school curriculum

blocks.summary: Reduce maternal mortality and improve sexual and reproductive health
blocks.rationale: The SRMNCAH&N Strategy 2024-2028 rolled out emergency obstetric care to all maternity facilities and skilled birth attendance rose to 93.4%; UNFPA notes maternal mortality remains high.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 101 — Eswatini: "Sexual Reproductive Maternal & Newborn Child, Adolescent Health & Nutrition (SRMNCAH&N) Strategy (2024–2028)"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 65 — UNFPA: "maternal mortality remained high"

recommendations.text: Allocate additional resources to end preventable maternal mortality and morbidity

Decriminalize the voluntary interruption of pregnancy in cases of rape, incest, serious malformation of the fetus or risks to the health or life of the pregnant woman, and guarantee access to sexual and reproductive health services
Accelerate efforts to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality rates, improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities

Implement commitments made at the Nairobi Summit, held to celebrate the twenty-fifth anniversary of the International Conference on Population and Development, to deliver quality health services, in particular maternal and neonatal care services, at all levels of care by improving the supply-chain management for reproductive health commodities in both public and private health facilities

blocks.summary: Improve access to quality education, retention and completion
blocks.rationale: Eswatini is implementing the Education Sector Strategic Plan 2022-2034 and competency-based curriculum reform, school feeding reaches 355,478 learners and the primary dropout rate fell from 6.5% to 4.8%; free secondary education is not yet provided.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 105 — Eswatini: "Education Sector Strategic Plan (ESSP) 2022–2034"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 117 — Eswatini: "a reduction in the national primary school dropout rate from 6.5% to 4.8%"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 114 — Eswatini: "Due to resource constraints, Eswatini is not yet ready to provide free secondary education"

recommendations.text: Prioritize effective coordination and investment in primary, secondary, vocational and tertiary education to ensure access and quality outcomes
Increase investment in the education sector to enhance quality and accessibility of education to all
Continue taking measures to improve the functioning of the education system, allowing pregnant girls access to education, and make education free and compulsory for 12 years of schooling
Further promote the right to education of children through the implementation of national programmes to address dropout rates
Advance efforts to finalize the draft strategy to address the increasing school dropout rates

blocks.summary: Introduce free secondary education
blocks.rationale: The National Report states that Eswatini is not yet ready to provide free secondary education; a task team is studying standardised fees.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 114 — Eswatini: "Due to resource constraints, Eswatini is not yet ready to provide free secondary education"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 118 — Eswatini: "MOET commissioned an Education Sector Transformation Task Team to develop innovative means for standardising secondary school fees"

recommendations.text: Continue national efforts related to the reopening of schools and consider ensuring free education from the eighth to twelfth grades
Adopt a coherent strategy to ensure compulsory free education up to the age of 16 to ensure that there are fewer dropouts
Continue enhancing its efforts towards pursuing rights to education and consider introducing a free education policy at the secondary school level

blocks.summary: Maintain access to education during the COVID-19 pandemic
blocks.rationale: Radio, television, print and blended learning reached about 70% of enrolled learners, all public schools reopened under health protocols and a Learning Passport platform was introduced.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 111 — Eswatini: "These interventions reached approximately 70 % of enrolled learners"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 112 — Eswatini: "MoET introduced the Learning Passport, a digital platform providing continuous access to curriculum-based learning during emergencies"

recommendations.text: Study ways to improve children’s continued access to education in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, to maintain the country’s development course

blocks.summary: Menstrual hygiene management to combat school dropout
blocks.rationale: The documents contain no information on this recommendation.

recommendations.text: Pursue its efforts to combat school dropout by ensuring sound menstrual hygiene management for girls in vulnerable situations

blocks.summary: Women's economic empowerment and shelters
blocks.rationale: A National MSME Policy 2024-2029 and the Citizen Economic Empowerment Act 2023 support women's enterprises; shelters remain privately operated.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 65 — Eswatini: "The National MSME Policy 2024–2029 promotes the formalisation of informal enterprises"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 64 — Eswatini: "the Government is making efforts to establish a state-owned gender-based violence shelter"

recommendations.text: Continue to promote the rights of women and girls

Invest in additional efforts to improve the system of protection of women in need by establishing shelters or temporary accommodation and educational centres for women in need, and in their economic empowerment
Further strengthen economic empowerment initiatives, especially for women and youth

Continue to support the economic emancipation of women while expanding its scope to cover all development spheres in accordance with the strategic road map of the Government for the period 2019 to 2022
Continue to implement the women-driven economic empowerment initiatives under the auspices of the Strategic Roadmap 2019–2023

blocks.summary: Align legislation with CEDAW and combat gender stereotypes
blocks.rationale: All ministries were directed to review legislation for CEDAW compliance under the Programme of Action and ILO Conventions 100 and 111 were ratified; the Family Law Bills have not been enacted and customary law still entrenches inequality.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 22 — Eswatini: "all government ministries are directed to review their respective pieces of legislation to promote the objects and purposes of CEDAW"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 24 — Eswatini: "Eswatini ratified ILO Conventions Nos. 100 and 111"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 79 — United Nations country team: "customary law entrenched gender inequality in inheritance and property rights"

recommendations.text: Take further measures to implement the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, in particular to curb discrimination and violence against women
Repeal all legal provisions that perpetuate gender stereotypes and discrimination against women
Adopt the necessary measures to combat occupational segregation and gender stereotypes in the working world
Continue efforts to end all forms of discrimination and violence against women and girls

blocks.summary: Domesticate CEDAW and align family and succession laws
blocks.rationale: CEDAW is not incorporated into domestic law and the Marriages Bill 8 of 2022 and Matrimonial Property Bill 9 of 2022 are still not enacted; the Government itself requests support for the Family Law Bills.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 21 — Eswatini: "While CEDAW has not yet been fully incorporated into domestic law, the Government is progressively aligning national laws with the Convention’s provisions"

National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 128 — Eswatini: "The Government requires technical and financial support for the full operationalisation of the Legal Aid Act, the Commission on Human Rights and Public Administration Bill, and the comprehensive Family Law Bills"

recommendations.text: Establish the legal framework for the domestication of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women

Make further efforts to bring the legislation into compliance with the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, to enable women’s enjoyment of fundamental human rights, such as the right to property and inheritance

Take action to align all laws and policies with the principle of equality and non-discrimination, as stated in the Constitution and in accordance with Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women
Ensure that the national legislation is in line with the international and regional instruments, particularly concerning the elimination of discrimination against women

themes.theme: Rights related to name, identity & nationality

blocks.summary: Equal rights of mothers and fathers to transmit nationality
blocks.rationale: No reform is reported; the UN country team recommends amending section 43 of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 111 — United Nations country team: "amend section 43 of the Constitution on citizenship by birth and the Citizenship Act, 1992, to remove gender-discriminatory provisions"

recommendations.text: Guarantee, through appropriate legislative measures, equal rights to fathers and mothers with regard to the transmission of nationality to children

blocks.summary: Combat violence against women and implement the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act
blocks.rationale: Eswatini adopted a GBV Coordination Mechanism, trained frontline responders, expanded one-stop centres and runs five (privately operated) safe houses; the UN country team and civil society report persistently high GBV and weak enforcement.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 58 — Eswatini: "The DPMO has adopted a formalised Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Coordination Mechanism"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 64 — Eswatini: "five safe houses are operational across the country, all of which are privately operated"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 80 — United Nations country team: "high rates of gender-based violence persisted due to weak enforcement, cultural barriers and limited funding"

recommendations.text: Make further efforts, including by raising public awareness, to enforce the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act of July 2018 to protect women’s rights and to end violence against women and girls
Redouble efforts to combat violence against women by developing legislation in this area
Take all necessary measures, both in law and in practice, to combat violence against women
Continue efforts to combat violence in all its forms and intensify awareness campaigns against practices that are harmful to children and women or that prevent their full upbringing

Continue its strategies and approaches in ending all forms of discrimination and violence against women and girls through effective implementation of the National Strategy and Action Plan to End Violence
Increase the necessary efforts to end all forms of violence against women and children, in particular sexual and domestic violence
Implement the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act, 2018, and adopt regulations to eliminate gender-based and domestic violence
Accelerate the implementation of the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act to ensure substantive protection of women from sexual and domestic violence, particularly in the context of COVID-19
Effectively apply the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act, 2018, fulfilling its commitment made at the Nairobi summit in 2019
Ensure better protection of women and girls against sexual violence
Strengthen the coordination of public authorities in the protection of women and children against sexual violence
Continue efforts to combat sexual crimes and domestic violence
Strengthen the implementation of the policies and the legal framework to eradicate harmful traditional practices that discriminate against women and the girl child
Adopt legislation which will effectively criminalize and combat sexual offences and domestic violence

blocks.summary: Review nationality laws to guarantee women equal rights
blocks.rationale: No reform is reported; the UN country team recommends amending section 43 of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 111 — United Nations country team: "amend section 43 of the Constitution on citizenship by birth and the Citizenship Act, 1992, to remove gender-discriminatory provisions"

recommendations.text: Review the Constitution and law on nationality in order to guarantee women equal rights as men

blocks.summary: Prevent forced and child marriage
blocks.rationale: Civil registration officials were trained to detect forced and child marriages, customary-marriage observers (umgijimi) check age and consent, and child marriage is prohibited by the Children's Protection and Welfare Act 2012; the minimum age of marriage is not yet 18.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 122 — Eswatini: "has trained officials to detect potential forced or child marriages during the registration process of marriages"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 124 — Eswatini: "child marriage is explicitly prohibited under the Children’s Protection and Welfare Act of 2012"

recommendations.text: Continue to ensure the full protection of young girls against harmful practices and forced marriages

themes.theme: Participation of women in political & public life

blocks.summary: Increase women's participation in decision-making
blocks.rationale: Women hold 29% of parliamentary seats after the 2023 elections (four elected under the Election of Women Members Act 2018) and 25% of Cabinet.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 54 — Eswatini: "women holding 29 per cent of seats in the Parliament, with 25% held in the Cabinet"

recommendations.text: Pursue the policy of eliminating inequalities between men and women by taking additional measures to increase the participation of women in political and public life, in particular in decision-making positions
Continue to combat the unequal representation of women in decision-making positions
Redouble efforts in promoting women’s participation and representation in politics and decision-making processes
Intensify efforts to increase the participation of women in political decision-making positions
Implement a minimum quota of 30 per cent for the representation of women in the House of Assembly, to ensure the representation of the women in decision-making process

blocks.summary: Participation of women, children, persons with disabilities and local communities in climate frameworks
blocks.rationale: NDC 3.0 sets dedicated targets for women, youth and persons with disabilities in climate governance bodies, a youth consultation forum was held and the Disaster Risk Management Act (2025) was enacted through multi-sectoral consultation.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 29 — Eswatini: "3.0 adopts an inclusivity and Just Transition approach, with dedicated targets for women, youth, and PWDs in climate governance bodies"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 30 — Eswatini: "The Disaster Risk Management Act 16 of 2025 was enacted through multi-sectoral stakeholder consultations"

recommendations.text: Ensure the meaningful participation of women, children, persons with disabilities, and local communities in the development and implementation of climate change and disaster risk reduction frameworks

blocks.summary: Prohibit corporal punishment in all settings
blocks.rationale: Corporal punishment remains lawful in the home, alternative care, day care, schools and penal institutions.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 17 — Committee on the Rights of the Child: "was seriously concerned that corporal punishment was still lawful in the home, in alternative care settings, in day care, in schools and in penal institutions"

recommendations.text: Prohibit all corporal punishment at home, in alternative care settings, day care, schools and penal institutions
Take practical steps, including through legislative measures, to put an end to corporal punishment in all settings, especially against children
Enact legislation that explicitly prohibits corporal punishment of children in every setting

blocks.summary: Raise the minimum age of marriage to 18
blocks.rationale: The Marriages Bill 8 of 2022 has not been enacted; the Committee on the Rights of the Child urges its adoption.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 23 — Eswatini: "the Government has prioritised the enactment of a suite of Family Law Bills"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 89 — Committee on the Rights of the Child: "urged Eswatini to revise its legislation, including by amending the Marriage Act and adopting the marriage bill, in order to ensure that the minimum age of marriage was established at 18 for both girls and boys"

recommendations.text: Finalize the review of the Marriage Act which will raise the marriageable age to 18 from 16 for both males and females

blocks.summary: Child-protection systems and free education
blocks.rationale: Additional social workers and community child protection committees were deployed and free primary education guaranteed; the CRC finds no integrated child protection system.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 120 — Eswatini: "The DPMO has reinforced additional social workers and community child protection committees"

recommendations.text: Centre recovery efforts, among others, on child-protection systems, to step up the fight against violence against children and guarantee access to free education

themes.theme: Persons with disabilities: definition, general principles

blocks.summary: Protect the rights and education of persons with disabilities
blocks.rationale: The National Disability Advisory Council was established (2023), the NDPA 2024-2028 adopted and disability grant beneficiaries rose to 17,193; the UN country team notes accessibility gaps and a resourcing need.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 9 — Eswatini: "The establishment of the National Disability Advisory Council in 2023"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 73 — Eswatini: "The Disability Grant beneficiaries increased from 5 019 in 2021 to 17,193 in 2025"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 97 — United Nations country team: "accessibility gaps persisted in buildings, transport and information"

recommendations.text: Continue to take measures to ensure an adequate standard of living for persons with disabilities
Allocate adequate resources and funding for the full implementation of the relevant legislative framework to protect the rights of persons with disabilities
Continue efforts to protect the rights of persons with disabilities, and to eliminate any discrimination against them
Continue consolidating its successful policies to guarantee the right to education for persons with disabilities
Accelerate and improve access to education for children with disabilities

blocks.summary: Protect human rights defenders, journalists and activists
blocks.rationale: The National Report says no one is targeted; investigations into the killing of lawyer Thulani Maseko have stalled and Eswatini has no legal framework for the protection of defenders.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 46 — Eswatini: "Eswatini provides a safe environment for exercising civic space rights, with no individuals targeted"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/2), para. 24 — United Nations country team: "investigations had stalled in relation to the perpetrators of the 2021–2023 violence in which protestors, including a prominent human rights lawyer, had been killed"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 66 — JS5: "Eswatini did not have a comprehensive legal framework for the protection of human rights defenders"

recommendations.text: Prevent and ensure accountability for attacks, repression and intimidation against journalists, human rights defenders and peaceful protesters
Protect human rights defenders, journalists and all social activists
Guarantee de jure and de facto the free exercise of the legitimate work of political opponents, human rights defenders and journalists

Ensure the protection of human rights defenders and journalists so that they can carry out their work without any type of reprisals and ensure respect of freedom of expression, association and peaceful protests

blocks.summary: Withdraw charges against defenders under the Suppression of Terrorism Act and repeal the Act
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: The Act was upheld by the Supreme Court (August 2024) and continues to be used; Amnesty and El Hak call for charges to be dropped.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/1), para. 47 — Eswatini: "the Supreme Court upheld the Sedition and Subversive Activities Act 46 of 1938 and Suppression of Terrorism Act 3 of 2028 as consistent with constitutional guarantees"

Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/SWZ/3), para. 58 — Amnesty International: "withdraw all charges brought solely under the Suppression of Terrorism Act that related to the peaceful exercise of the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly"

recommendations.text: Withdraw all criminal charges brought against human rights defenders and political opponents under the Suppression of Terrorism Act of 2008, and repeal or amend this act

meta.caveat: The Human Rights Committee's follow-up procedure grades only the two to four “priority” recommendations it selected from this country's Concluding Observations (CoBs). The other CoBs are not graded.

paragraphs.title: Violence against women
paragraphs.recommendation: The State party should: (a) Promptly adopt legislation to effectively criminalize and combat sexual offences and domestic violence; (b) Provide relevant actors in the police, public prosecution and judiciary with training on sexual and gender-based violence and on evidence-gathering for such cases; (c) Strengthen its efforts to raise the awareness of the wider public to the adverse impact of sexual and gender-based violence and encourage reporting, inter alia by systematically informing women and children of their rights and of the existing legal avenues through which they can receive protection; (d) Ensure that all cases of sexual and gender-based violence are thoroughly investigated, that perpetrators are prosecuted and, if convicted, are punished with appropriate sanctions, and that victims receive full reparation; (e) Ensure that victims have access to effective remedies and means of protection, including to an adequate number of psychological and educational centres, and that other support services, such as accommodation or shelters, are available in all parts of the country. * Adopted by the Committee at its 130th session (12 October–6 November 2020)

limbs.eval: The Committee welcomes the enactment of the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act (No. 15) in 2018. It requests further information on (i) the coverage of the crime of “unlawful stalking” (part II.10) and the exception of “acceptable courting”; (ii) the reason for limiting the crime of abduction only to children, excluding adult women; (iii) whether marital rape is considered an unlawful act in the legislation; and (iv) the definition of “domestic violence” (part XII) and whether it complies with the Covenant. The Committee welcomes the State party’s efforts to conduct training sessions. It requests, however, more information on the demonstrated impact of these sessions and additional planned initiatives to train police officers, judicial officers, medical services personnel and social welfare officers. The Committee welcomes the continuous awareness-raising campaigns on gender-based violence. It requires information on (i) the live phone-in programme on TV and how confidentiality is ensured to victims of gender-based violence; (ii) the accessibility and impact of such a campaign; and (iii) statistics from the past three years on the number of complaints received related to sexual and gender-based violence

The Committee requires information on the dates of the establishment of the unit for sexual offences, cases of domestic violence and child protection in the Royal Police Service and the specialized unit on protection and in charge of sexual offences and cases of domestic and gender-based violence in the office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. The Committee also requires statistical information on the number of investigations, prosecutions and convictions of cases of sexual and gender-based violence, the sanctions imposed and the reparations granted to victims. The Committee requires information on the measures taken by the State after the Committee adopted its concluding observations to ensure that all victims have access to effective remedies and means of protection. In this regard, the Committee requires updated information on plans to establish one-stop centres in the four regions of the country and the measures taken to ensure that women victims of violence are provided with support services, including with accommodation and shelters in all parts of the country

paragraphs.title: Freedom of expression, assembly and association
paragraphs.recommendation: The State party should prevent and redress attacks on human rights defenders and other social activists and promptly adopt legislation to ensure that any restriction on the exercise of freedom of expression, assembly and association complies with the strict requirements in the Covenant. The State party should take all measures necessary to protect the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly and ensure that police officials, judges and prosecutors receive adequate training regarding such protection

limbs.eval: The Committee welcomes the adoption of the Public Order Act No. 12 (2017) and the Code of Practice on Gatherings Notice No. 201 (2017). It requests, however, information on the application of such legislation and that the State comment on information received according to which additional requirements and restrictions not included in the Act are also applied in the case of gatherings. It also requests information on measures taken to prevent and redress attacks on human rights defenders and other social activists. The Committee also requests information on the adoption of the Swaziland Broadcasting Bill 2016, currently under review, and updated information on the issuing of broadcasting licences. In this regard, it requires information on the planned fees that will be imposed for the application and registration of radios, particularly of community radio stations, and whether they are compatible with the Covenant. The Committee notes the launch of a second mobile network operator, expanding the media space, although it still requires information on the rules imposed on the ownership and control of radio and television stations, and whether they comply with the Covenant

paragraphs.title: Participation in public affairs, and corruption
paragraphs.recommendation: The State party should bring its constitutional framework into compliance with the Covenant, including with article 25, inter alia by: (a) Fostering a culture of political pluralism, ensuring freedom of genuine and pluralistic political debate, and allowing the registration of opposition political parties, including to contest elections, field candidates and participate in the formation of government; (b) Undertaking a constitutional reform process with the objective of devolving power to democratically elected branches of government, and guaranteeing the right of every citizen to take part in the conduct of public affairs and have access to public service on general terms of equality; (c) Guaranteeing free and fair elections; (d) Ensuring the independence and effectiveness of the bodies in charge of elections and anti-corruption

limbs.eval: The Committee takes note of the information provided by the State party, but requests more information on measures taken, since the adoption by the Committee of its concluding observations, to ensure a culture of political pluralism, to ensure a genuine and pluralistic political debate, and to allow the registration of opposition political parties, including to contest elections, field candidates and participate in the formation of the Government. The Committee takes note of the information provided. It reiterates its recommendation with respect to the need to undertake a constitutional reform process with the objective of devolving power to democratically elected branches of government, and guaranteeing the right of every citizen to take part in the conduct of public affairs and have access to public service on general terms of equality. While taking note of the information provided by the State party, the Committee requests information on the measures taken since the adoption of its concluding observations to guarantee free and fair elections. The Committee takes note of the information provided by the State party, particularly on the current lack of financial independence of bodies in charge of elections and anticorruption measures. It requests information on the measures taken since the adoption of its concluding observations to ensure the operational and financial independence of the said bodies. The Committee reiterates its recommendation. Recommended action: A letter should be sent to the State party informing it of the discontinuation of the follow-up procedure. The information requested should be included in the State party’s next periodic report. Next periodic report due: 28 July 2021. 6
